This allows you to target actual nutritional deficits safely without taking nutrients your body already has in abundance.

Ritual Essential Protein is a single-source pea protein formula. Each serving contains 20g of protein and 400mg of L-Methionine. The company states that L-Methionine is added to the pea protein to provide a complete amino acid profile. Each serving provides 8g of essential amino acids (EAAs) and 4g of branched-chain amino acids (BCAAs), with leucine at 1,785mg, isoleucine at 1,063mg, and valine at 1,124mg. Pea protein naturally has low methionine, which is why Ritual adds it, but the product does not include extra leucine beyond what pea protein naturally contains.

Whey protein has traditionally been considered superior for muscle building because of its fast absorption and complete amino acid profile. It enters the bloodstream faster than plant-based proteins and has high levels of BCAAs like leucine, isoleucine, and valine, which support muscle growth and repair. However, a 2024 crossover trial found that plant-based protein supplements often have lower leucine and EAA content, which may make them less effective at stimulating muscle protein synthesis than animal-based proteins, but combining plant proteins can improve the EAA profile. The study showed that a plant-based blend with added leucine stimulated muscle protein synthesis similarly to whey protein, and plant proteins with higher leucine content promote anabolism to a level similar to animal-based proteins. The trial also found that 20g of a pea and canola protein isolate blend increased muscle protein synthesis above baseline but not as effectively as whey—only when leucine content was matched did it perform equally to whey.

A 2025 systematic review concluded that single-source plant proteins generally offer limited benefits compared to whey, especially in acute recovery, but well-formulated plant protein blends such as pea, rice, and canola can stimulate muscle protein synthesis at levels comparable to whey when consumed in adequate amounts (≥30g with ~2.5g leucine). In contrast, a 12-week resistance-training study found that when soy and whey were matched for leucine content, there were no meaningful differences in outcomes over time—despite conflicting reports on plant vs. animal protein efficacy, soy and whey supplements matched for leucine comparably supported strength increases and muscle growth over 12 weeks.

Ritual’s leucine content of ~1,785mg per serving is below the ~2,500-3,000mg threshold that several studies suggest is needed for plant protein to match whey’s acute muscle-protein-synthesis response gram-for-gram. Whey isolate typically delivers ~2,000-2,700mg leucine per equivalent serving. Ritual’s addition of methionine addresses the issue of incomplete amino acid profiles in plant proteins, but it does not directly address the leucine gap through fortification, unlike some research-backed plant blends.

For general daily protein intake, satiety, and overall health, Ritual’s pea protein is a solid, complete option. Plant protein digests more slowly, which some people find easier on digestion, and this product includes 3 grams of dietary fiber, which may help increase satiety, as well as added iron and choline. For maximizing post-workout muscle protein synthesis, it is likely less potent per 20g serving than a leucine-rich whey isolate, based on dose-response research—though the difference could be reduced by taking a larger serving or combining it with other leucine-containing foods. The consensus in recent literature is that plant protein can be as effective as whey for muscle building, but only when the formula compensates for pea protein’s naturally low leucine content, either by blending protein sources or adding leucine. Ritual fills the methionine gap but not the leucine gap.

If the goal is maximal anabolic response per scoop, a leucine-fortified plant blend or whey isolate may have a slight advantage. If the goal is a clean, allergen-friendly, complete-amino-acid daily protein with added micronutrients, Ritual is a well-formulated option that should perform similarly to whey in most everyday situations.

Sometimes—but not automatically. A gummy can contain the same amount of a vitamin as a pill if the serving size and Supplement Facts panel say so. The form itself doesn’t inherently make the ingredient weaker or stronger.

Gummies often contain fewer nutrients, especially iron, calcium, magnesium, and sometimes vitamin B12 or vitamin D, because some ingredients are difficult to stabilize or make palatable in gummy form. Dose per serving may be several gummies, not one. Compare the labeled serving—not the number of pieces. Quality can vary more by brand and product. Dietary supplements aren’t FDA-approved for safety, effectiveness, or label accuracy before sale. fda.gov

Limited studies suggest absorption is generally similar for some nutrients, while vitamin D gummies may even be absorbed better than tablets in one small study; that does not mean all gummies are better. pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov

Gummies commonly contain added sugar or sugar alcohols and can be easier to overeat.

Practical advice: Compare the exact nutrient amounts and forms, and choose a product with independent quality verification such as USP Verified or NSF Certified when available. If you need a medically important dose—particularly iron, folate during pregnancy, vitamin D, or B12—a tablet or capsule may offer more predictable dosing, but check with a clinician.

It can be independently verifiable—but the words alone are not proof. In the U.S., “third-party tested” is not a standardized government certification or guarantee. A company may mean that an outside laboratory tested a raw ingredient, one production batch, or the finished product. The label usually does not tell you which laboratory performed the testing, whether the lab was independent or hired directly by the manufacturer, what was tested—identity, potency, microbes, heavy metals, pesticides, banned drugs, etc.—whether every batch was tested, or whether the results apply to the specific lot you purchased. FDA does not pre-approve supplements or routinely test them before sale; manufacturers are responsible for safety, quality, and truthful labeling. fda.gov

What makes the claim more credible is a named, recognizable certification program, such as USP Verified, which includes facility auditing, documentation review, laboratory testing, and ongoing off-the-shelf testing. dev.usp.org NSF Certified / NSF Contents Certified evaluates whether the contents match the label and screens for specified contaminants; NSF says it conducts periodic retesting and audits. nsf.org NSF Certified for Sport adds screening for substances prohibited in sport. nsf.org ConsumerLab is an independent testing organization, though its detailed results are generally accessed through its own service rather than a universal certification seal.

Then verify the product in the certifier’s online directory, checking the exact brand, product, dosage form, and current status. A “GMP-certified facility” claim is useful but does not necessarily mean that the specific finished product was independently tested.

Treat an unqualified “third-party tested” statement as a marketing claim until the company provides evidence. Ask for the name of the lab, the tests performed and acceptance criteria, a certificate of analysis for the specific lot, the lab’s accreditation—ideally to ISO/IEC 17025—and confirmation that testing was on the finished product, not merely an ingredient. Even a legitimate test only supports the properties tested; it does not prove the supplement is effective, risk-free, or appropriate for you. Also, FDA does not approve supplements for safety or effectiveness before marketing. fda.gov

Yes—plant protein can build muscle and support recovery, but whey has a small “per gram” advantage, especially for stimulating muscle-protein synthesis after a workout. Ritual Essential Protein can be an effective option if you use enough total protein and calories.

Ritual Essential Protein contains pea protein with added L-methionine, while whey protein is milk-derived. Ritual Essential Protein provides 20 g of protein per serving, whereas whey usually provides 20–30 g. Pea protein is relatively strong among plant proteins, and Ritual adds methionine to address a limiting amino acid. Whey is complete and naturally rich in essential amino acids. Leucine is usually lower in plant protein per gram compared to whey, which typically has higher levels and helps trigger muscle-protein synthesis. For muscle gain, plant protein is effective, especially with adequate serving size and total intake, though whey is slightly more efficient per gram. Ritual Essential Protein is dairy-free and may suit people avoiding lactose, while whey isolate is low in lactose and concentrate contains more. The best choice depends on preference: Ritual for vegan/dairy-free preference, tolerability, taste, and sustainability; whey for maximizing protein quality and convenience per calorie/dollar.

Ritual lists 20 g of pea protein per serving and adds L-methionine to improve the amino-acid profile. ritual.com

For long-term strength and muscle gain, plant protein is often close to whey provided the dose is adequate. In a 12-week resistance-training trial, pea protein produced changes in strength and muscle mass comparable to whey. pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov A 2024 study also found that a plant-protein blend stimulated post-exercise muscle-protein synthesis similarly to whey when participants consumed 32 g of protein. pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov

However, in acute laboratory studies, a plain plant-protein dose can produce a lower muscle-protein-synthesis response than whey because it generally provides less leucine and some essential amino acids. Adding leucine—or using a well-formulated blend—can make the response similar to whey. pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov

For general nutrition, Ritual’s 20 g serving is perfectly reasonable. For maximizing muscle gain, whey has the edge, but Ritual can work well if you consume roughly 25–35 g protein per meal/shake, depending on body size and your total daily intake. Aim for approximately 1.4–2.0 g protein per kilogram of body weight per day if you train regularly. pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov If using Ritual, consider taking it with a meal or using a larger serving if the label and your calorie goals allow. Your training quality, total daily protein, calories, sleep, and consistency matter much more than whether the powder is plant- or dairy-based.

Bottom line: Choose whey if you tolerate dairy and want the most efficient protein per gram. Choose Ritual if you prefer plant-based protein—it is a legitimate muscle-building option, not a second-rate substitute.

Not consistently. While gummy vitamins can deliver essential vitamins, they rarely offer the exact same accuracy, stability, or complete nutritional profile as traditional pills (tablets or capsules).

Several key differences explain why gummies often fall short compared to traditional vitamins.

Inconsistent Nutrient Dosage. Because gummies are soft and moist, nutrients (especially water-soluble ones like Vitamin C and B vitamins) degrade much faster in a gummy than in a dry, compressed pill. To offset this degradation and ensure the product still meets label claims by its expiration date, manufacturers often over-fortify gummies by adding up to 150%–250% of the active ingredients. As a result, fresh gummies may contain significantly more active nutrient than what is listed on the bottle, which can carry toxicity risks for fat-soluble vitamins (like Vitamin A or D). Older gummies near their expiration date may have degraded to contain less than the listed amount. Independent laboratory tests (such as those by ConsumerLab.com) consistently show that gummy vitamins fail label-accuracy tests far more often than standard pills or capsules.

Missing Key Nutrients. Gummy vitamins often lack important minerals or contain them in very small amounts. Ingredients like iron, calcium, and magnesium are bulky and have strong metallic or chalky tastes that ruin the flavor and texture of a gummy. If you need specific minerals—especially iron (for anemia) or high doses of calcium—a traditional pill or softgel is almost always necessary.

More Lenient Regulatory Standards. Because gummies are notoriously difficult to manufacture accurately, organizations like the United States Pharmacopeia (USP) allow wider dosage tolerances for gummies than for traditional pills. For example, gummies are allowed higher overages of certain vitamins without violating quality standards compared to tablets.

Added Sugars and Fillers. To make them taste good, gummies typically contain added sugars or corn syrup (usually 2–8 grams per serving). Sugar alcohols (like erythritol or xylitol), which can cause stomach upset or digestive distress in sensitive individuals. Citric acid, which enhances flavor but can erode tooth enamel over time.

Does Your Body Absorb Gummies the Same Way? Yes, in terms of absorption, gummies work. Assuming a gummy actually contains the promised amount of a nutrient, your digestive system absorbs vitamins from gummies just as effectively as—if not slightly faster than—traditional pills. Additionally, gummies avoid the rare issue of hard-compressed pills failing to break down properly in the stomach. The primary issue with gummies isn't absorption, but rather dosage accuracy and ingredient completeness.

The Bottom Line. Use traditional pills/capsules if you want precise dosing, a complete range of vitamins and minerals (including iron and calcium), and no added sugars. Use gummy vitamins if you suffer from pill fatigue, have trouble swallowing pills, or otherwise wouldn't take your vitamins at all. A gummy with slightly variable dosages is still better than no nutrition at all, provided you stick to the recommended serving size.

In the U.S., a higher price does not legally require a supplement to meet a higher purity standard. For dietary supplements, the FDA sets baseline requirements under its current good manufacturing practice rules, including controls intended to ensure identity, strength, composition, purity, and limits on contamination. Those requirements generally apply regardless of whether a product costs $10 or $100. fda.gov The FDA does not pre-approve supplements or routinely test every product before sale. The manufacturer is responsible for compliance, and FDA primarily inspects, monitors, and takes action when problems are identified. fda.gov A premium price may reflect more extensive batch testing, better raw-material sourcing, a more expensive formulation, higher doses, or independent certification—but price alone is not evidence of any of those things.

Better indicators of quality include a credible third-party certification, such as USP Verified; USP says its program includes facility audits, documentation review, laboratory testing, and ongoing off-the-shelf testing. test.usp.org A publicly available certificate of analysis (COA) tied to the specific lot—not merely a generic claim that the product is “tested”—is also helpful. Clear disclosure of ingredient forms and amounts, rather than a proprietary blend, is another factor. Evidence of testing for relevant contaminants—such as heavy metals, microbes, pesticides, or adulterating drugs—appropriate to that product is also important.

Bottom line: Regulation establishes a baseline, not a price-based hierarchy. A more expensive supplement can be better tested, but you need independent verification or transparent testing documentation to know.

I'll research both phones' camera specifications and expert comparisons to give you an accurate answer.  
The iPhone 17 Pro and the Samsung Galaxy S26 Ultra are extremely close in camera performance, but the iPhone 17 Pro edges ahead overall, particularly for reliability, video, and low-light consistency — while the S26 Ultra wins on raw zoom range and detail resolution.  

The iPhone 17 Pro has a 48MP wide camera with f/1.78 aperture at 24mm equivalent, plus a 48MP ultrawide at f/2.2, and a 48MP 4x telephoto at f/2.8, 100mm equivalent, both with sensor-shift OIS. All three rear cameras now offer 24MP shooting capability, and can also shoot at the full 48MP.  

The Galaxy S26 Ultra features new lenses with wider apertures on the 200MP main sensor and the 50MP 5x telephoto, running on the Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5. Its full array is a 200-MP wide-angle camera with an f/1.4 aperture, a 50-MP ultrawide with f/1.9 aperture, a 10-MP 3x telephoto at f/2.4, and a 50-MP 5x telephoto at f/2.9.  

DxOMark found the iPhone 17 Pro secured a lead over the Galaxy S26 Ultra, despite Samsung's 200MP sensor with f/1.4 aperture increasing light intake by 47% compared to its predecessor. The site summarized it as a divergence in approach: Samsung prioritized optical power and zoom range, offering the market's best hardware for distance, while Apple focused on the instantaneous user experience — the iPhone 17 Pro remains the benchmark for daily reliability and refined processing.  

Testing showed the S26 Ultra still trails the iPhone 17 Pro in challenging low-light scenes, with Samsung's device showing more visible luminance noise and slightly less detail in portraits captured in dim environments.  

Interestingly, in daylight if compared to the iPhone 17 Pro, the S26 Ultra's lower image resolution in bright light conditions leads to poorer fine details reproduction than the Apple flagship.  

DxOMark noted that autofocus accuracy can sometimes struggle when detecting faces on the S26 Ultra.  

For Samsung, the 3x telephoto is so-so with its detail while the 5x is more like good, though the 3x telephoto is a class or two below the other cameras at night; stabilization is about as good as it gets.  

Samsung's zoom hardware is objectively stronger — the 5x telephoto reaches up to 5x optical zoom versus Apple's 4x, and the ultra-wide-angle lens with macro capability extends to up to 2,300 millimeters in the digital zoom range. Apple counters somewhat with computational zoom, as its tetraprism telephoto lens is capable of 4× optical zoom and up to 8× "optical-quality" zoom through sensor cropping.  

Both cameras now sit essentially tied on independent scoring — the iPhone 17 (non-Pro) even ties the Galaxy S26 Ultra on DxOMark's leaderboard with a score of 157 points, ranking 20th globally, and DxOMark gave the standard iPhone 17 an overall score of 157, putting it in 20th place globally, tied with the iPhone 16 Pro, Oppo Find X7 Ultra, and Galaxy S26 Ultra. The Pro model scores even higher than the base iPhone.  

If you prioritize consistent, reliable photos with excellent low-light performance and class-leading video (ProRes, Dolby Vision, Log), the iPhone 17 Pro is the safer choice. If you want maximum zoom flexibility and highest resolution stills for cropping, the Galaxy S26 Ultra's hardware gives it an edge in versatility — though it requires more manual tweaking to get the best results.

The Galaxy S26 Ultra is the better all-around camera system if you value zoom, detail, versatility, and low-light photography. The iPhone 17 Pro is the better choice for video, natural color, moving subjects, and consistently good results with minimal tweaking.

The Galaxy S26 Ultra wins in main-camera detail due to its 200MP main sensor and stronger crop/detail potential. For zoom, the Galaxy S26 Ultra has a dedicated 3x and 5x telephoto lenses, plus up to 100x digital zoom. The Galaxy S26 Ultra also has a 50MP ultra-wide camera compared to the 48MP ultra-wide on the iPhone. In low light for stills, the Galaxy S26 Ultra has a slight edge thanks to its wider f/1.4 main aperture and f/2.9 5x telephoto, which improve light capture. For color and skin tones, the iPhone 17 Pro is preferred due to more restrained and natural-looking processing. The iPhone 17 Pro is superior for video with better stabilization, HDR consistency, audio, and pro-video formats. The iPhone 17 Pro also offers more reliable point-and-shoot performance with predictable exposure and motion capture. For selfies and video calls, the iPhone 17 Pro has an 18MP Center Stage camera with autofocus and strong video features.

The iPhone 17 Pro has three 48MP rear cameras, including a 4x telephoto that provides an optical-quality 8x option, while Samsung uses a 200MP main camera, 50MP ultra-wide, 3x telephoto, and 5x telephoto. apple.com

Choose the Galaxy S26 Ultra if you frequently shoot at 5x–10x zoom, want the most flexible camera setup, photograph landscapes, buildings, concerts, or distant subjects, prefer brighter and more vivid images, or take lots of night or astrophotography. Independent testing generally finds Samsung ahead in zoom and specialized still photography, while the iPhone remains stronger or more balanced for video. Tom’s Guide named the S26 Ultra its current top camera phone, but TechRadar still ranks the iPhone 17 Pro Max—whose camera system matches the 17 Pro—higher for overall photo/video balance. tomsguide.com

Choose the iPhone 17 Pro if you record a lot of family videos, travel videos, or social content, want excellent results without adjusting settings, prefer natural colors and skin tones, need ProRes, Apple Log 2, or strong audio/video workflows, or already use a Mac, AirDrop, iCloud, or Final Cut Pro.

My verdict:  
Best still-photo camera: Galaxy S26 Ultra  
Best video camera: iPhone 17 Pro  
Best camera for most serious creators: iPhone 17 Pro  
Most versatile camera phone overall: Galaxy S26 Ultra

The clock time does not matter much for most people — what matters more is how you take the multivitamin. It is generally recommended to take your multivitamin with a meal or shortly after eating, which helps enhance the absorption of fat-soluble vitamins like A, D, E, and K, as they are better absorbed in the presence of dietary fats. Some experts specifically suggest taking supplements with your largest meal of the day, such as lunch or dinner, ideally containing some fat (think fatty fish, avocado, eggs, or nuts) to allow optimal absorption of the fat-soluble vitamins. The best approach is to start by evaluating your current routine and identifying the most consistent meal time in your day — that's typically the best time to take a multivitamin, regardless of whether it's morning, afternoon, or evening, since consistency trumps specific timing for most people. If you do take it without food, taking a multivitamin before bed is better than not taking it at all — absorption only drops by about five to ten percent if you take them in the evening or without food and water.

Morning may be better if you have B-vitamins in your formula, since morning doses may work better if your multivitamin includes B vitamins, which are directly linked to how your body converts food into energy. You may also prefer morning intake if you're sensitive to stimulating effects — some people find that taking a multivitamin too close to bedtime can disrupt their sleep due to the potential energizing effects of certain vitamins, like B-complex vitamins, so if this is a concern, consider a morning or midday dose instead. Evening may be better if you have a sensitive stomach in the morning — evening multivitamin intake works better for some individuals, particularly those with sensitive stomachs in the morning — if you experience nausea or digestive discomfort with morning vitamins, switching to evening might help. Evening may also be preferable if your dinner has more fat than breakfast — your evening meal often contains more dietary fat than breakfast, which can improve absorption of fat-soluble vitamins. Evening may also be better if your evenings are simply more reliable — nighttime consumption often wins for consistency, since evening routines tend to be more stable and less hurried than morning schedules — and consistency is crucial for maintaining steady nutrient levels.

There's no one-size-fits-all "best time" to take a vitamin. Pick whichever time you can pair reliably with a meal (for absorption) and stick to every day — that matters far more than "AM vs. PM." If you're on medications or have specific health conditions, it's worth checking with a doctor or pharmacist, since individual health conditions, medications, and lifestyle can impact the best time to take supplements.

Gummy vitamins generally contain less active ingredient per serving than pills, and their dosing is often less accurate or consistent. Chewable tablets can contain up to 50% active ingredients by weight, while gummies are limited to about 10% due to the need for added sugars, sugar alcohols, corn starch, and food dyes to achieve the right texture. A two-gummy serving may provide less than 60% of most vitamins compared to a chewable tablet serving that provides 100% or more.

Independent testing has shown discrepancies between label claims and actual content in gummy supplements. ConsumerLab tests found that some gummy multivitamins contain less than or much more than their listed amounts. The FDA/USP allows vitamin C in gummies to reach up to 250% of the label amount, compared to a 150% limit for tablets. In ConsumerLab's 2023 testing, all four gummy multivitamins reviewed had potency inaccuracies—one had significantly less vitamin D than claimed, and three had nearly double their stated folic acid. This failure rate is higher than the roughly 30% seen across all multivitamin formats. More broadly, testing indicates that more than 25% of multivitamins may have inaccurate ingredient quantities, with gummy vitamins being especially prone to such issues.

Formulating gummies with consistent potency is more difficult. It can be harder for manufacturers to include the same amount of vitamins in a gummy as in a pill, and gummy potency may decline faster due to moisture sensitivity. Companies may add twice or three times as much of certain nutrients during production because they expect breakdown over time, which explains why some nutrients like folic acid can far exceed label claims. The gel-like structure of gummies can also result in slight variation in active ingredient amounts from one gummy to the next.

One exception involves vitamin D absorption. When the dose matches, gummies are not necessarily worse, and for vitamin D specifically, they may absorb better. A crossover study in healthy adults given 20,000 IU of vitamin D3 found greater bioavailability with gummies compared to tablets. A follow-up study found the area under the concentration curve was higher with gummies than tablets (1474 ng·h/mL vs. 774 ng·h/mL), likely due to the oil/emulsifier matrix in gummies aiding absorption of fat-soluble vitamins. For water-soluble vitamins such as B12, folate, and vitamin C, a bioequivalence pilot study found no significant difference in total B12 or folate exposure between gummy and tablet multivitamin formulations, but only if the actual amount in the gummy matches the label.

Pills generally contain more active ingredient per serving and are more space-efficient than gummies. Pills and tablets tend to be more consistent and reliable in terms of label accuracy, while gummies have a documented history of both under- and over-dosing. When doses are equal, water-soluble vitamins absorb similarly in both forms, and gummies may have an advantage for fat-soluble vitamins like D. Gummies also have a shorter shelf life because moisture and oxygen can degrade nutrients faster than in pills, worsening the accuracy issue over time.

If precise, guaranteed dosing is important, such as for a specific medical need, pills are the safer choice. For general supplementation where some variability is acceptable, quality gummies from reputable, third-party-tested brands can still be effective enough for many people.

There's no single absorption number for multivitamins because bioavailability differs dramatically by nutrient, dose, formulation, and your own body. That said, here's what the evidence shows.

Absorption rates for individual nutrients in a multivitamin can range enormously. Vitamin A: the absorption of preformed vitamin A from dietary supplements can be as high as 90%. Vitamin C: up to 90% of vitamin C may be absorbed at moderate intakes, while at higher doses, absorption is less than 50%. Vitamin K1: is considered roughly 80% bioavailable in synthetic purified form, according to research compiled in a comparative bioavailability review. Biotin: true (corrected) ileal digestibility of biotin for synthetic purified biotin was 94% in pig studies. Folic acid: is generally assumed to be about 85% bioavailable when added synthetically to food, per bioavailability research. Vitamin B12: is the standout exception — absorption drops sharply as dose increases. One study found bioavailability, as a function of dose, was significantly different between 2.5, 5, and 10 µg doses at 50.9 ± 32.5%, 26.7 ± 22.3%, 15.4 ± 13.6%, respectively. This is because the bioavailability of crystalline vitamin B12 through active absorption is reported to have a maximum capacity of 1.5–2.5 µg per dose, so B12 doses far beyond that (like the 500–1000 mcg often found in supplements) mostly aren't absorbed through the normal active pathway.

The bioavailability from multivitamins can be quite low for fat-soluble micronutrients like vitamins A, D, E, K, and essential minerals such as iron and calcium, depending on how they are encapsulated, and what they are encapsulated with. There's even a risk that iron oxidizing vitamin A once dissolved in the stomach can degrade it before it's absorbed. Taking these with a meal containing some fat significantly helps absorption.

One frequently cited estimate suggests up to 90% of liquid vitamin nutrients might be absorbed, while only 10-20% from pills may be absorbed due to factors like digestion and solubility — though this specific claim should be taken with some caution since exact absorption is hard to measure and varies by nutrient.

For many water-soluble vitamins (like vitamin C or B-vitamins), the body actually does absorb them efficiently, but then excretes what it doesn't need through urine rather than never absorbing it in the first place. As one nutrition source pointed out, the body's homeostatic mechanisms regulate this — for example, homeostatic mechanisms regulate absorption or excretion depending on the nutrient status of the host (e.g., the iron status of the host affects iron absorption). So if you're already sufficient in a nutrient, your gut may simply absorb less of it or your kidneys filter out the excess — this isn't "waste" in a wasteful sense, it's the body protecting against overload.

Yes, generally. Despite imperfect absorption, research shows that nutrients from supplements get absorbed into our bodies to help fill nutritional gaps, and in some cases, the amount absorbed from supplements can be higher than that absorbed from food. Population data backs this up too: the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey reports that people taking multivitamins have a greater chance of getting the recommended intakes of almost all micronutrients.

Take multivitamins with food, especially one containing some fat, since fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K) are absorbed best when taken with a meal that contains dietary fat. Avoid taking nutrients that compete for absorption (like iron and calcium) at the same time. Be aware that gut health, medications, and individual conditions can drastically change absorption — some people genuinely absorb certain vitamins (like B12) very poorly regardless of dose or form.

A meaningful portion of most multivitamin nutrients does get absorbed and used — it's not mostly "flushed away" as popular myth suggests. But the efficiency varies wildly by nutrient (roughly 15–90%+), and very high doses of things like B12 or vitamin C show diminishing absorption returns, meaning megadosing often just produces expensive urine rather than added benefit.

When comparing the iPhone 17 Pro and the Samsung Galaxy S26 Ultra, the Samsung Galaxy S26 Ultra offers better overall battery life. 

It is important to note the hardware tier distinction here: the Galaxy S26 Ultra is Samsung’s largest flagship (matching up against Apple’s iPhone 17 Pro Max), whereas the standard iPhone 17 Pro is Apple’s smaller 6.3-inch device. 

Breakdown of performance comparison:

The Samsung Galaxy S26 Ultra features a 5,000 mAh battery paired with the Snapdragon 8 Gen 5 chip. The larger chassis allows for a significantly bigger battery capacity. The iPhone 17 Pro features a ~4,252 mAh battery (eSIM version) / ~3,998 mAh (physical SIM variant). While Apple's A-series chips remain exceptionally efficient, the physical size limit restricts total milliamp-hour capacity.

In standard web browsing and mixed-use drain tests, the S26 Ultra typically lasts around 16 hours of continuous active screen use. In real-world daily scenarios, users see anywhere from 7 to 8+ hours of screen-on-time (SOT), comfortably spanning a day and a half for moderate users. The iPhone 17 Pro reaches around 15.5 hours in benchmark web-browsing tests. In typical day-to-day mixed use (messaging, camera, social media, navigation), it delivers about 6 to 7 hours of screen-on-time. It easily gets through a full work day, but drops off faster under heavy stress than the S26 Ultra.

The Galaxy S26 Ultra supports upgraded 65W wired fast charging, reaching around 80–84% charge in just 30 minutes and a full charge in under 45 minutes. The iPhone 17 Pro reaches about 50–60% charge in 30 minutes via USB-C PD.

The verdict is that the Galaxy S26 Ultra wins. Its physically larger battery capacity gives it an edge in total battery life and screen-on time over the smaller iPhone 17 Pro. Note on the Pro Max: If battery life is your top priority and you are open to Apple's larger size option, the iPhone 17 Pro Max (~18 hours) actually outlasts the S26 Ultra. For most people, morning or midday with a meal is considered the ideal time to take a multivitamin. However, the single most important factor is consistency—the best time to take your multivitamin is whenever you can consistently remember to take it every day.

Here is a breakdown of why timing matters, the benefits of morning vs. night, and how to get the most absorption out of your supplement.

Why Morning (with Breakfast or Lunch) is Usually Best

Enhanced Absorption with Food: Multivitamins contain fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, and K), which require dietary fats to be absorbed properly by your body. Taking your multivitamin alongside a meal that contains healthy fats (like eggs, avocado, nuts, or yogurt) maximizes their effectiveness.

Energy Production: Multivitamins contain B vitamins, which help convert food into cellular energy. Taking B vitamins in the morning aligns with your body’s natural circadian rhythm and daytime energy needs.

Prevents Stomach Upset: Certain minerals and vitamins—particularly iron, zinc, and vitamin C—can cause nausea, cramping, or digestive upset if taken on an empty stomach. Taking them with a substantial breakfast or lunch helps buffer your stomach lining.

Potential Drawbacks of Taking it at Night

Sleep Disruption: Because B vitamins support energy metabolism, taking them right before bed can occasionally cause mild stimulation, vivid dreams, or difficulty falling asleep for sensitive individuals.

Empty Stomach Risk: If you take your multivitamin right before bed long after dinner, you risk absorbing less of the fat-soluble vitamins and potentially waking up with nausea or an upset stomach.

When Nighttime Might Make Sense

Evening Meals: If your breakfast is light (or you skip it entirely) and dinner is your main meal containing healthy fats, taking your multivitamin with dinner may offer better overall absorption.

Managing Nausea: If your multivitamin causes stomach discomfort even when taken with breakfast, taking it with a hearty evening meal might help you sleep through any minor digestive irritation.

Summary Checklist for Best Results

Take it with food: Always pair your multivitamin with a meal or snack that contains some fat (e.g., olive oil, peanut butter, cheese, or eggs).

Drink plenty of water: Water aids in swallowing and helps process the water-soluble vitamins (B-complex and C).

Be consistent: Build it into an existing habit, such as right after breakfast or alongside your lunch routine.

(Note: If your multivitamin contains specific high doses of iron or calcium, be aware that calcium can interfere with iron absorption. If you take separate individual mineral supplements, ask your doctor or pharmacist about spacing them out.)

Yes, a significant amount of the nutrients in standard multivitamins ends up being wasted. However, "wasted" happens in two distinct ways: either your body fails to absorb the nutrient in the first place, or your body absorbs it but excretes the excess because it doesn't need it. Here is a breakdown of why so much of a multivitamin goes to waste and what determines how much your body actually uses.

Water-Soluble vs. Fat-Soluble Vitamins (The "Expensive Urine" Effect): Your body handles vitamins in two main ways. Water-Soluble (Vitamin C and B-Complex): Your body cannot store large amounts of these. Once your blood levels reach saturation, your kidneys filter out the excess and flush it out through your urine (which is why your urine often turns bright neon yellow after taking a B-complex). If you already get enough B vitamins and Vitamin C from food, almost 100% of the extra amount in the multivitamin is wasted. Fat-Soluble (Vitamins A, D, E, and K): These are stored in your body's fat tissues and liver. They are not excreted in urine as easily, but they require dietary fat to be absorbed in the digestive tract. If you take a multivitamin containing Vitamin D or E on an empty stomach or with a fat-free meal, your body will absorb very little of it.

Form and Quality (Bioavailability): "Bioavailability" refers to how easily your body can break down and use a specific nutrient. Cheap, mass-market multivitamins often use cheaper synthetic forms of vitamins and minerals that have low bioavailability. Magnesium: Many multivitamins use magnesium oxide, which is cheap but has an absorption rate as low as 4% to 10%. Higher-quality forms like magnesium glycinate or citrate are absorbed much better. Folic Acid vs. Methylfolate: Synthetic folic acid must be converted by the liver into an active form. A large portion of the population carries a genetic variation (MTHFR mutation) that makes this conversion inefficient. Pill Disintegration: Some cheap, heavily compressed tablets don't even break down completely in the digestive tract before passing through the body.

Nutrient Competition: Multivitamins pack dozens of vitamins and minerals into a single pill, but certain minerals compete for the exact same pathways and receptors in your gut. High amounts of calcium block the absorption of iron and zinc. High amounts of zinc can interfere with copper absorption. When you take them all at the exact same time in large doses, they hinder each other's absorption.

The Body’s Natural Regulation: Your digestive tract actively regulates absorption based on your baseline needs. For example, if your body is low in iron, your gut will absorb a higher percentage of the iron you consume. If your iron levels are already adequate, your gut actively blocks high iron absorption to prevent toxicity. With Vitamin C, if you take a small dose (under 100 mg), your body absorbs roughly 80–90% of it. If you take a massive 1,000 mg dose, absorption drops to under 50%, and the rest is excreted.

Does this mean multivitamins are useless? Not necessarily, but they are not a replacement for a balanced diet. For healthy adults with a varied diet: Most of a multivitamin will indeed be wasted, providing little to no measurable health benefit. For specific groups: Multivitamins or targeted supplements are beneficial for people with specific needs, such as pregnant women (folic acid/folate to prevent birth defects). Older adults (who often struggle to absorb Vitamin B12 and need Vitamin D). Vegans/Vegetarians (who need B12 and sometimes iron). People with diagnosed deficiencies (e.g., low Vitamin D or anemia) or malabsorption conditions (like Celiac disease, Crohn's, or post-gastric bypass).

How to maximize absorption if you take supplements: Take them with food: Specifically a meal that contains healthy fats (like eggs, avocado, nuts, or olive oil) to absorb fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K). Prioritize targeted supplements over generic multivitamins: Instead of a mega-dose multivitamin, get bloodwork to see what you actually lack (e.g., just Vitamin D or Iron) and supplement only those. Look for absorbable forms: Check labels for chelates (e.g., magnesium glycinate instead of oxide, or methylated B-vitamins). Get nutrients from whole food first: Nutrients in food come with natural enzymes, fiber, and co-factors that help your body absorb them far more efficiently than a pill.

When comparing the cameras on the **iPhone 17 Pro** and the **Samsung Galaxy S26 Ultra**, declaring an absolute winner depends heavily on what you value most in mobile photography and videography. Both represent the peak of smartphone camera technology, but they lean into different strengths.

The **iPhone 17 Pro** focuses on realistic color accuracy, natural skin tones, and consistent exposure control across all lenses. Apple’s image pipeline default captures photos in high-detail 24MP, resulting in very natural textures and reliable dynamic range without looking overly processed. The **Galaxy S26 Ultra** uses a 200MP main sensor paired with a wide aperture ($f/1.4$) that collects roughly 47% more light. It leans toward punchier, more vibrant colors and higher default sharpening. While its standard binned 12MP photos hold great detail, it also gives you the option to shoot full 200MP frames for heavy cropping. The **iPhone 17 Pro** has the edge for natural skin tones and consistent colors; the **Galaxy S26 Ultra** has the edge for punchy contrast and fine-detail resolution.

The **iPhone 17 Pro** features a high-resolution 48MP telephoto lens (up to 4x optical zoom), providing sharp mid-range photos and excellent portrait compression. However, quality drops off significantly past 10x to 15x digital zoom. The **Galaxy S26 Ultra** employs a dual-telephoto system (3x 10MP lens and a 50MP periscope lens offering up to 10x optical-quality reach). For distance shots (10x, 30x, and up to 100x Space Zoom), Samsung easily outperforms Apple with cleaner detail and enhanced AI stabilization. The **Galaxy S26 Ultra** has the edge by a wide margin for long-distance optical/digital zoom.

The **iPhone 17 Pro** uses aggressive multi-exposure processing indoors and in low light. Night mode is fast, smooth, and reduces noise remarkably well without blowing out highlights. The **Galaxy S26 Ultra**, benefiting from its wider aperture main sensor ($f/1.4$), captures more light physically before processing even kicks in. In near-total darkness and dedicated Astrophotography modes (via Expert RAW), the **Galaxy S26 Ultra** retains sharper shadow details and captures star fields better. The **Galaxy S26 Ultra** has the edge for night skies and low-light detail retention.

The **iPhone 17 Pro** continues to lead in overall video performance. It offers superior overall video stabilization, better dynamic range when transitioning light levels, and higher-fidelity spatial audio/microphones. For filmmakers, ProRes Log remains the industry-standard smartphone format for heavy color grading. The **Galaxy S26 Ultra** has narrowed the gap substantially, introducing features like APV Log directly inside the stock camera app, Horizon Lock stabilization, and Audio Eraser capabilities. However, motion blur and low-light video noise are still handled slightly better by Apple. The **iPhone 17 Pro** has the edge for video consistency, stabilization, and color-grading workflows.

Get the **iPhone 17 Pro** if you prioritize class-leading video recording, point-and-shoot simplicity, realistic skin tones, and color consistency across all three lenses. Get the **Galaxy S26 Ultra** if you want superior zoom performance, an expansive set of manual controls (Expert RAW, stock Log options), stronger astrophotography, and high-megapixel flexible cropping options.

No — under U.S. regulation, price has no bearing on the purity or quality standard a supplement must meet. The regulatory floor is the same for all supplements, regardless of price. Short answer: No. Regulatory purity standards for dietary supplements have nothing to do with price. In the U.S., the FDA regulates all dietary supplements under the same set of Current Good Manufacturing Practice (cGMP) rules, codified at 21 CFR Part 111 — whether the product costs $8 or $80.

What the regulation actually requires (uniformly, for everyone): Under Part 111, manufacturers of dietary ingredients must confirm identity before use, and finished products must meet specifications for identity, purity, strength, and composition. Specifically, manufacturers must confirm the identity of every dietary ingredient before it enters production, verifying the ingredient is what it claims to be. Finished product testing requires identity, purity, strength, composition and limits on contaminants as established in product specifications. Under 21 CFR 111.75(c), companies must test or examine one or more established finished product specifications for identity, purity, strength, composition, and limits on contaminants that may adulterate the product to verify the manufacturing process yielded a compliant batch. For raw materials, all raw materials must be tested and verified to confirm their identity, purity, strength, and composition before use in production.

This baseline applies identically to a store-brand fish oil capsule and a premium boutique brand — the law doesn't create tiers of purity requirements based on retail price.

The reason more expensive supplements sometimes have better purity or fewer contaminants isn't because a higher price triggers a stricter legal standard — it's because enforcement is inconsistent. FDA doesn't pre-approve supplements before sale (unlike drugs), and inspections/enforcement are resource-limited, so compliance varies by manufacturer regardless of price point. Common violations found by FDA include "Raw materials were not being tested for identity", which can happen at any price tier. Third-party certification costs money. Programs like USP Verified, NSF Certified for Sport, or ConsumerLab testing are voluntary and paid for by the manufacturer — these add real cost and are often (but not always) more common in pricier products. But these are voluntary seals, not government mandates. Sourcing and testing frequency are business choices. A company can legally meet the 21 CFR 111 floor with minimal testing (e.g., relying on a single appropriate test per lot) or go well beyond it with more rigorous, frequent testing — and the latter costs more, which may get passed to the consumer.

The regulatory floor — the legal minimum purity/identity/strength standard — is the same for a $10 supplement and a $100 supplement. If you want actual evidence of higher purity, look for third-party certifications (USP, NSF, Informed-Sport, ConsumerLab) rather than assuming price itself reflects a different legal purity standard, because it doesn't.

It depends entirely on what is behind the phrase — "third-party tested" can be a rigorous, checkable fact, or it can be an empty marketing slogan. Here's the breakdown:

Legitimate third-party verification comes in two forms. First, certification with a public seal. An outside body tests the product and lets the brand display a seal you can verify, like USP or NSF. Recognized programs include NSF International, USP, Informed Sport/Informed Choice, BSCG Certified Drug Free, and ConsumerLab, each with different scopes, like purity, banned substance screening, and potency. Second, per-lot testing with a published Certificate of Analysis (CoA). The brand pays an accredited lab to test each batch and shows you the results. Both routes can be legitimate, but what's not legitimate is the phrase floating alone on a label with nothing behind it.

A seal on a bottle alone isn't proof — a photo of a seal on packaging can be faked or misused, so you should confirm the product and lot number in the certifier's online directory or contact the certifier directly. Practically, look up the certifier's public database. Check the certifying organization's website for a searchable database of certified products — legitimate certifications like USP Verified, NSF Certified for Sport, and Informed Choice maintain public databases with product details, batch numbers, and expiration dates. Match the exact product name and lot number on the certifier's site to what's on your bottle, since certifications are often issued per product/batch rather than per brand generally. Check testing frequency, which varies by program — for example, Informed Choice does monthly batch testing, NSF Certified for Sport does periodic retesting and unannounced audits, and USP Verified involves annual renewal with ongoing monitoring. Be suspicious of vague claims. Avoid products making generic "third-party tested" claims without specifying the testing laboratory. A real claim names the certifier or lab and lets you check.

Scope varies widely. Not all certifiers test the same things. For instance, among common programs: testing for substances prohibited in sport is done by BSCG Certified Drug Free and Informed Sport, but not by NSF or USP Verified, while contaminant testing is optional/extra for BSCG, included for NSF and USP Verified, but not covered by Informed Sport. Certification does not mean effectiveness. A certification means the label is honest, not that the product will work for you — quality and effectiveness are two different things. This matters because the FDA doesn't check first. The FDA does not approve dietary supplements before they're sold — it regulates them as food, leaving safety and labeling up to the manufacturer. That regulatory gap is exactly why third-party programs exist and why label accuracy problems are more common in uncertified products — research found that supplements without third-party testing were significantly more likely to contain contaminants. Retailers and sports leagues have their own bars. For example, Costco often requires NSF Certified for Sport for sports-nutrition placement, and products marketed to competitive athletes generally need banned-substance-specific certification (NSF Certified for Sport, Informed Sport, or BSCG) rather than a generic quality mark.

Bottom line: "Third-party tested" is verifiable if it points to a specific, named certifier or lab with a checkable database/CoA — you can independently confirm the product, lot number, and scope of testing. But when it's just printed text with no named lab, no seal, and no CoA offered, it's functionally an unverifiable marketing claim. The practical rule: trust the seal, then verify it yourself on the certifier's site rather than taking the label's word for it.

The short answer is yes—plant protein can be just as effective as whey protein for building muscle, supporting recovery, and improving strength.

For a long time, whey was considered superior because it naturally contains high levels of essential amino acids (EAAs)—especially leucine, the main trigger for muscle protein synthesis (MPS). However, modern sports nutrition research shows that when total daily protein intake and amino acid profiles are matched, plant protein produces the same gains in muscle size and strength as whey protein.

Here is a detailed breakdown of how plant protein compares to whey, and specifically how Ritual Essential Protein stacks up against traditional whey protein powders.

Historically, plant proteins had two main disadvantages compared to whey. First, lower bioavailability: plant proteins are slightly harder for the body to digest and absorb than whey isolate. Second, incomplete amino acid profiles: many single plant sources are lower in certain essential amino acids (e.g., pea protein is naturally lower in methionine and leucine compared to whey).

How science solved this: multiple clinical studies (including landmark trials comparing pea protein to whey) have demonstrated that when individuals engage in resistance training, pea protein vs. whey protein: a study published in the Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition found no statistically significant difference in muscle thickness or strength gains between participants taking pea protein versus whey protein over a 12-week training period. Total protein matters most: as long as you hit your daily protein targets (typically 1.6–2.2 grams per kilogram of body weight) and consume enough leucine per serving (around 2–3 grams), the source of the protein becomes far less important.

Ritual Essential Protein (specifically their flagship Daily Shake 18+) is formulated specifically to overcome the traditional drawbacks of plant protein.

Ritual Essential Protein (Pea) has organic yellow pea protein as the protein source, 20 grams of protein per serving, a complete amino acid profile (fortified with L-methionine to mimic animal protein completeness), ~4g BCAAs per serving, is vegan, gluten-free, soy-free, lactose-free, includes choline, iron, calcium, and is Informed-Sport Certified (tested for heavy metals and banned substances).

Standard Whey Protein (Isolate/Concentrate) has dairy (cow’s milk) as the protein source, 24–25 grams of protein per serving (typically), a complete amino acid profile (naturally rich in all 9 EAAs), ~5.5g BCAAs (higher natural leucine), contains dairy/lactose (concentrates contain more lactose than isolates), added micronutrients depend on brand (often fortified or unfortified), and third-party testing varies by brand.

Key strengths of Ritual: fortified amino acid profile: pea protein is naturally low in methionine. Ritual adds fermented L-methionine to ensure it provides a complete amino acid profile with all 9 essential amino acids required for optimal muscle recovery. Clean & traceable: Ritual is third-party tested by Informed-Sport and provides full supply-chain transparency (e.g., non-GMO organic peas sourced from the U.S.). Easier on the stomach for some: for people who get bloating, gas, or stomach cramps from whey (due to lactose sensitivity or milk proteins), pea protein is hypoallergenic and gentler on digestion.

Key strengths of whey: higher natural leucine content: whey naturally has higher leucine concentrations per gram, meaning you might need slightly less total whey powder per serving to hit the optimal threshold for muscle building. Cost efficiency: gram-for-gram of protein, quality whey protein is generally more affordable than premium plant-based options like Ritual. Texture and blendability: whey protein tends to dissolve more smoothly in liquid and has a naturally creamy texture, whereas plant proteins can sometimes feel slightly earthy or grainy.

Choose Ritual Essential Protein if: you follow a plant-based or vegan diet. You are lactose intolerant or experience digestive discomfort/bloating from dairy-based proteins. You prioritize clean-label transparency, organic ingredients, and third-party testing for heavy metals.

Choose Whey Protein if: you have no trouble digesting dairy or lactose. You want maximum protein per dollar spent. You prefer a smoother texture and higher natural leucine content without needing fortified amino acids.

Bottom line: from a physical results standpoint—whether your goal is building lean muscle mass, recovering after workouts, or managing weight—Ritual Essential Protein is just as effective as whey protein, provided your overall diet meets your daily protein needs.

The phrase "third-party tested" on a supplement label can be either a genuinely verifiable guarantee or just an unregulated marketing claim. It depends entirely on whether the manufacturer provides proof or relies on vague text.

Because the FDA does not approve dietary supplements before they go to market, manufacturers are largely responsible for their own quality control, and the term "third-party tested" is not strictly defined or regulated by law.

Here is how to tell the difference between a meaningless marketing claim and an independently verifiable test.

If a label simply prints the text "Third-Party Tested" or includes a generic checkmark logo without naming the testing organization, it is unverifiable.

In these cases, "third-party tested" could mean:  
Minimal or one-time testing: The company sent a single sample of raw material to a lab years ago, but doesn't test finished batches.  
Testing for the wrong things: They tested for heavy metals, but not for potencies, purity, or contaminants like micro-organisms.  
Unaccredited labs: They used a friend's lab or an unaccredited facility that doesn't follow standard testing protocols.  
Self-created seals: The company's graphic designer created a official-looking "Approved" or "Tested" seal that carries no regulatory weight.

A supplement's third-party testing claim is independently verifiable if it meets one or both of the following criteria.

A. A Recognized Certification Seal  
If a brand pays an independent, accredited organization to audit and test their products, the organization will allow the brand to display its official mark. You can independently verify these claims by visiting the certifier's public online database.

The most reputable third-party certification bodies include:  
USP (United States Pharmacopeia): Verifies that the product contains the ingredients listed on the label in the declared potency, does not contain harmful levels of contaminants, and breaks down properly in the body.  
NSF International (and NSF Certified for Sport): Verifies label accuracy and tests for contaminants. Certified for Sport also screens for over 280 athletic-banned substances.  
ConsumerLab.com: An independent testing organization that randomly tests off-the-shelf supplements and publishes reports on quality, purity, and disintegration.  
Informed-Choice / Informed-Sport: Focuses heavily on testing for banned substances and contamination for athletes.  
BSCG (Banned Substances Control Group): Offers protection against drug contamination and verifies ingredient quality.

B. Batch-Specific Certificates of Analysis (CoAs)  
Reputable brands that do not pay for full third-party certification logos often provide a Certificate of Analysis (CoA) for individual batches.  
Many brands place a QR code on the bottle linking to the CoA for that exact lot number.  
A valid CoA should come from an ISO/IEC 17025 accredited laboratory (the gold standard for testing laboratories).  
The CoA will show actual lab results for purity, heavy metals, microbial limits, and ingredient potency.

Red Flags to Watch For  
"Tested on Raw Materials Only": Some brands test raw ingredients when they buy them, but fail to test the final blended product for contamination or degradation during manufacturing.  
No Lot Number or Expiration Date: If a bottle lacks a lot/batch number, it is impossible to trace back to any specific lab test.  
In-House Testing Labeled as Third-Party: A company testing its own products in its own lab is first-party testing, not third-party.

Summary Checklist for Consumers  
To confirm a claim is real:  
Look for a known seal (USP, NSF, Informed-Choice, ConsumerLab).  
Verify on the certifier's site: Go to the certifier's website (e.g., nsf.org and search for the brand name in their public directory.  
Check for a CoA: Look for a QR code or lot search tool on the brand's site that pulls up third-party laboratory results from an ISO-17025 accredited lab.

No. By law, regulatory agencies do not hold higher-priced supplements to higher purity or quality standards than cheaper ones. Whether a dietary supplement costs $5 or $150, the legal standards governing its purity, identity, strength, and manufacturing process are exactly the same.

In the United States, for example, dietary supplements are regulated by the FDA under the Dietary Supplement Health and Education Act (DSHEA) and 21 CFR Part 111 (Current Good Manufacturing Practices, or cGMP). Under these regulations, all supplement manufacturers—regardless of retail price—must legally ensure that their products are pure and unadulterated, meaning free from hazardous levels of contaminants like heavy metals (lead, arsenic, mercury), pesticides, mold, or illegal drugs. They must also match the label by containing the exact ingredients listed on the label, in the amounts stated, throughout the product's shelf life. Additionally, they must follow cGMP standards, meaning they are manufactured, packaged, labeled, and held under controlled quality conditions. Regulatory agencies do not have "tier systems" or higher legal baselines for luxury or premium brands.

While a higher price does not trigger a higher regulatory standard, expensive brands may choose to do things voluntarily that increase their costs. However, price alone is not a guarantee of quality. Here is what price differences usually represent. Voluntary Third-Party Certification (Higher Quality Assurance): To stand out, some brands pay independent testing organizations (such as USP, NSF International, Informed-Choice, or ConsumerLab) to audit their facilities and test their batches. These seals guarantee that a third party verified the product's purity and potency beyond basic regulatory requirements. Ingredient Form and Bioavailability: Cheaper supplements often use cheaper raw materials (e.g., Magnesium Oxide, which is inexpensive but poorly absorbed). More expensive supplements might use higher-grade, chelated, or trademarked ingredient forms (e.g., Magnesium Glycinate or patented extracts like KSM-66 Ashwagandha), which cost manufacturers more to source. Higher-Quality Packaging and Sourcing: Expensive supplements may use dark glass bottles to protect light-sensitive nutrients, non-GMO or organic raw materials, vegan capsule shells, or allergen-free facilities. Marketing, Branding, and Profit Margins: A significant portion of a high-priced supplement's cost often goes toward sleek packaging, influencer marketing, ad campaigns, and retail markup—none of which improve purity.

The Bottom Line: Price Does Not Equal Purity. Cheap supplements from reputable, established store brands (like Kirkland Signature or Nature Made) often pass strict purity tests because they have massive supply chains and strict compliance protocols. Expensive supplements can still fail independent testing for heavy metals, inaccurate dosages, or contamination.

How to Verify Purity (Instead of Relying on Price): If you want to ensure high purity and quality, do not rely on the price tag. Look for third-party seals such as USP Verified, NSF Certified for Sport, or Choice/Informed-Sport printed directly on the label. Also, check for Certificates of Analysis (COAs): Quality-focused brands often publish lot-specific COAs on their websites showing third-party lab testing results for heavy metals and contaminants.

Whether the iPhone 17 Pro Max is worth the jump over the iPhone 17 Pro comes down to battery life, screen real estate, and hand comfort, as Apple has kept performance and camera systems identical across both models.

Apple standardizes the core tech across both phones. Both run on the A19 Pro chip paired with 12GB of RAM and vapor-chamber thermal cooling. The camera system is identical triple 48MP setup (48MP Main, 48MP Ultrawide, 48MP Periscope Telephoto). Both have matching aluminum-titanium hybrid construction with identical color options (including Cosmic Orange, Deep Blue, and Silver). They share the same ProMotion 120Hz displays, Ceramic Shield glass, and fast USB-C/MagSafe charging speeds.

The iPhone 17 Pro has a 6.3-inch display, weighs 206 g (7.27 oz), and measures 150.0 x 71.9 x 8.75 mm. Its battery capacity is ~4,000–4,250 mAh. Storage options are 256GB, 512GB, and 1TB. The starting price is $999. The iPhone 17 Pro Max has a 6.9-inch display, weighs 233 g (8.22 oz), and measures 163.4 x 78.0 x 8.75 mm. Its battery capacity is ~4,800–5,080 mAh. Storage options include 256GB, 512GB, 1TB, and 2TB. The starting price is $1,199.

Buy the iPhone 17 Pro Max if you want maximum battery life. The Pro Max houses a noticeably larger battery capacity, easily providing all-day-plus or 2-day battery life for heavy users compared to the standard Pro. Choose it if you consume a lot of media or game heavily. The massive 6.9-inch display provides an immersive screen for watching videos, mobile gaming, and reading large documents or spreadsheets. Stick with the iPhone 17 Pro if you prefer one-handed use. At 6.3 inches and 206 grams, the 17 Pro is far easier to handle, slide into small pockets, and use comfortably without wrist fatigue. Since the cameras and processor are unchanged, you aren't missing out on feature capability by picking the smaller Pro.

The iPhone 17 Pro offers several improvements over the iPhone 16 Pro. If you're buying new, get the 17 Pro. If you already own a 16 Pro, the upgrade is solid but not essential — it’s worth it if battery life, telephoto camera, or charging speed are concerns; otherwise, it’s skippable if you’re satisfied with your current device.

The iPhone 17 Pro has a brighter and less reflective display, better cooling, a faster chip with more RAM, and longer battery life. The frame is now a laser-welded aluminum unibody with an Apple-designed vapor chamber for improved thermal performance. Some reviewers say the new shape feels more comfortable in hand, though others prefer the premium finish of the titanium 16 Pro model — there's something slightly more premium in the way the old model is finished.

Performance is powered by the A19 Pro chip, replacing the A18 Pro. Real-world testing shows the iPhone 17 Pro delivers significant improvements in performance over the already powerful 16 Pro across all tests, with meaningful gains in CPU performance stability, though GPU stability improvements are more modest.

The display brightness increases to 3,000 nits from 2,000 nits, and with an anti-reflective cover, the iPhone 17 Pro is much easier to read outdoors.

Battery and charging see the biggest real-world gains. The iPhone 17 Pro rates at 33 hours of video playback compared to 27 hours on the 16 Pro — a 22% improvement — and wired charging increases to 40W from 20W, cutting full charge time by about 50%. However, some anecdotal early testing suggests Apple's claims for video playback are much better for the 17 generation, while third-party battery life tests for normal use show only a minor improvement.

The telephoto camera changes from a 12MP 5x zoom to a 48MP 4x zoom. The front camera sees a larger upgrade — the 17 Pro can take landscape selfies with the phone held in portrait, at 18MP with a wider lens to fit more people in frame, and while pixel-level quality is similar, the 17 Pro wins on versatility. Apple also added simultaneous front and rear video capture with Dual Capture.

Connectivity includes an update to a newer Bluetooth version, and reviewers highlight Connectivity: N1 steals the show as a notable but under-the-radar improvement.

The 16 Pro still holds its ground in some areas. The speakers on the 17 Pro are worse than the 16 Pro — the 16 Pro is louder and more balanced, while the 17 Pro has more bass but less midrange and lower volume. As with the iPhone 17, there is no longer a 128GB version on the 17 Pro, so budget-conscious buyers lose that entry option. The 17 Pro also carries a higher base price in some markets, per Cult of Mac's comparison.

For users coming from a 16 Pro or newer, upgrades may feel minor — the iPhone 17 Pro does offer better battery life, an improved telephoto camera, a wider selfie camera, and open-gate video recording. One comparison tool put it bluntly: mostly no — the difference is too small to matter in everyday use, and the overall difference is not big enough to justify updating.

For users upgrading from iPhone 14 Pro or older or buying fresh, the 17 Pro is the clear choice for filming, editing, and portability. If you're choosing between the two as a new purchase, for the same launch price you get three-sensor 48MP camera consistency, 40W fast charging, six more hours of battery, and the new ceramic back — if you're buying new, the 17 Pro is clearly the better pick.

The arrival of a new iPhone doesn't suddenly make last year's model any less capable — the iPhone 16 Pro remains a powerful, reliable device that will continue to serve most users extremely well. Upgrade if battery anxiety, selfie/vlogging quality, or charging speed are pain points for you; otherwise, save your money and wait another cycle.

The best iPhone for someone switching from Android depends slightly on which Android phone you’re coming from and your budget, but for most switchers, the best overall choices are either the **iPhone 15 Pro / iPhone 16 Pro** or the base **iPhone 15 / iPhone 16**.

Here is a breakdown of the best options based on your priorities, along with key features that make the transition easier for Android users.

The best overall for Android switchers is the **iPhone 15 Pro or iPhone 16 Pro**. If you are coming from a mid-to-flagship Android phone (like a Samsung Galaxy S series, Pixel Pro, or OnePlus), **you should go with a Pro model.** The **120Hz ProMotion Display** matches the smooth-scrolling screens found on most Android phones released in recent years. Standard iPhones (15 and 16) are still capped at 60Hz, which can feel laggy to a former Android user. The Pro models give you that smooth 120Hz feel you're used to. The **USB-C Port** means you won't need to replace all your Android charging cables, as Apple switched to USB-C starting with the iPhone 15 series. The **Action Button** is a customizable button that Android users love—you can map it to launch your camera, turn on the flashlight, or trigger custom shortcuts.

The best value or best standard option is the **iPhone 16 or iPhone 15**. If you don't care about a 120Hz refresh rate and want to save money while still getting modern features, the standard **iPhone 15** or **iPhone 16** is the sweet spot. **USB-C standard** allows easy charging with your existing gear. The **Dynamic Island** replaces the old notch with an interactive cutout for notifications, media controls, and turn-by-turn navigation (similar to Android multitasking widgets). It also offers **great performance and battery life**, as iOS is well-optimized, meaning battery life is excellent right out of the box.

The best budget option is the **iPhone SE (3rd Gen) or standard iPhone 13/14**. If you want to test the iOS waters without spending a lot, the **iPhone 13/14** still offers great performance and cameras, but keep in mind these use the older **Lightning connector**, so you'll need different charging cables. The **iPhone SE** has a classic design with a home button, best if you want the absolute cheapest modern iOS experience.

Key things to know before you switch include **RCS Support in iMessage (iOS 18+)**. Texting between Android and iPhone is no longer as frustrating. iPhones now support RCS, meaning high-res photos/videos, typing indicators, and read receipts work when messaging your remaining Android contacts. **Google Apps Work Great on iOS.** You don't have to give up Google Services. Google Maps, Gmail, Google Photos, Google Drive, and Chrome work seamlessly on iOS—and in some cases, Google apps update on iOS before Android. **Home Screen Customization (iOS 18)** now lets you place app icons anywhere on the grid, tint app icons, and customize your Control Center—features Android users have enjoyed for years, making iOS feel much more familiar. For **Data Transfer**, download Apple's **"Move to iOS"** app on your Android device *before* setting up the new iPhone. It will wirelessly transfer your contacts, message history, photos, videos, web bookmarks, and free apps.

Quick recommendation summary: **Coming from a flagship Android (Galaxy S23/S24, Pixel 7/8/9 Pro)?** $\rightarrow$ Get the **iPhone 15 Pro or 16 Pro** (to keep the 120Hz display). **Coming from a mid-range or budget Android?** $\rightarrow$ Get the **iPhone 15 or iPhone 16** (best value, modern USB-C design).
