When comparing mapping and navigation, Roborock is the clear winner overall, primarily due to the underlying technology it uses.

Here is a detailed breakdown of how the two brands compare across key navigation metrics.

Roborock (LiDAR / Laser Navigation): Most Roborock models use PreciSense LiDAR (a spinning laser turret on top of the vacuum). It bounces light off walls and objects to measure distance with millimeter accuracy.  
Roomba (Camera / vSLAM): Premium Roombas (like the j7, j9, and s9 series) rely on Visual SLAM (vSLAM), using optical cameras (often with an LED headlight on j-series models) to take pictures of your ceilings, furniture, and surroundings to build a map.

Mapping Speed & Accuracy  
Winner: Roborock  
Roborock: Can map an entire floor of your home in 5 to 10 minutes using its quick-mapping mode before it even starts cleaning. The maps are extremely precise right out of the box.  
Roomba: Requires multiple cleaning or "mapping runs" around the house to build an accurate layout, which can take hours or even days depending on the size of your home.

Dark / Low-Light Navigation  
Winner: Roborock  
Roborock: Because LiDAR uses lasers, it works flawlessly in complete darkness. You can schedule it to run at night while you sleep with all the lights off.  
Roomba: Camera-based navigation requires ambient light to see. While newer models like the Roomba j7/j9 have front LED headlights to help in the dark, they can still slow down, struggle to orient themselves, or get lost in dimly lit rooms.

Path Efficiency & Logic  
Winner: Roborock  
Roborock: Navigates in neat, hyper-efficient, straight-line grid patterns. It rarely bumps into walls or furniture at high speed because the laser detects them beforehand.  
Roomba: While modern Roombas do clean in logical lines (unlike early random-bump models), they rely more heavily on physical bumpers to register obstacles, leading to a slightly slower, more aggressive cleaning path.

Obstacle Avoidance (Small Items & Pet Waste)  
Winner: Tie (Model-Dependent)  
Roomba (j7 / j9 Series): Roomba’s PrecisionVision Navigation (front-facing camera + AI) is legendary for small obstacle detection. iRobot even offers the P.O.O.P. (Pet Owner Official Promise), guaranteeing a replacement if the j7/j9 runs over pet waste.  
Roborock (MaxV / Reactive AI Models): Higher-end Roborocks (like the S8 MaxV Ultra or Qrevo MaxV) combine LiDAR with front RGB cameras and 3D structured light. They are equally adept at recognizing shoes, cords, socks, and pet waste.

Low-Clearance Furniture (Under Beds & Couches)  
Winner: Roomba  
Roomba: Because Roombas do not have a raised laser turret on top, they tend to be lower in profile (~3.4 to 3.6 inches tall). They can fit under lower-clearance furniture.  
Roborock: The LiDAR dome makes most Roborocks slightly taller (~3.8 to 4.0 inches tall), which may prevent them from fitting under certain low couches or cabinets.

Summary Verdict

| Feature | Roborock | iRobot Roomba |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Primary Sensor** | LiDAR Laser | Optical Camera |
| **Initial Mapping Speed** | **Fast** (5–10 mins) | **Slow** (Multiple runs) |
| **Dark Room Cleaning** | **Excellent** | **Fair to Good** |
| **Path Efficiency** | **Extremely Precise** | **Good** |
| **Obstacle Avoidance** | **Excellent** (MaxV models) | **Excellent** (j7/j9 models) |
| **Low Furniture Clearance** | ~4.0 inches | **~3.5 inches** |

Buy a Roborock if: You want the fastest mapping, pinpoint navigation accuracy, effortless night/dark cleaning, and an efficient cleaning cycle.  
Buy a Roomba if: You have low-clearance furniture that a LiDAR turret would bump into, or you prioritize top-tier pet waste avoidance (Roomba j7/j9).

Robot vacuums and traditional upright vacuums perform differently, and testing shows a clear difference in deep-cleaning ability. Upright vacuums are significantly better at cleaning carpets. According to testing data cited by Vacuum Wars, the average deep clean score for upright vacuums is around 98% of embedded sand picked up, compared to robot vacuums where the average amount picked up is only 75%. This means a good upright can remove nearly all debris from carpet, while a robot might pick up only about three-quarters at best. Consumer Reports found an even starker gap in one head-to-head test: on embedded debris, the Miele upright picked up more than half of the debris, while the Samsung robovac picked up less than 20 percent, proving that for deep cleaning, a bot is no match for a traditional vacuum. The main reason is suction power: one aspect where an upright vacuum cleaner is miles ahead of a robovac is the suction power they offer — an average upright is a lot more powerful in terms of suction than any robotic vacuum cleaner. Robots also lose efficiency on thick carpet — robotics are best for uncluttered rooms with bare floors or low-pile rugs, since they generally use more power to navigate over thick carpet, which can drain the battery faster. Consumer Reports' 2026 testing reaffirms this: while upright and canister vacuums are better at deep-cleaning hardwood and carpets, a robot vacuum can be useful for regular touch-ups, and while they aren't as powerful as upright or canister vacuums, the best robotic vacuums are great for regular touch-ups and spot cleaning.

Robots do have strengths. On hard floors, they perform well. One vacuum expert notes robots are "as good or better than any other kind of vacuum at picking up debris on hard floors, and they can also mop hard floors as well," whereas uprights were originally built with carpet in mind. Robots are also better at cleaning under furniture: robot vacuums can be better than standard vacs at cleaning hard-to-reach spots such as under the bed or sofa, which matters if you have mobility issues or heavy furniture you don't want to move.

Most experts view the two types as complementary rather than interchangeable. Consumer Reports' own testing engineer sums up robots' sweet spot as: "Robotics are best for uncluttered rooms with bare floors or low-pile rugs." Robots require more daily maintenance — you'll need to do some prep work to move clothes, toys, and other objects off the floor before sending out the vacuum, and their smaller dustbins mean more frequent emptying. If you have wall-to-wall carpet, pets that shed heavily, or want truly deep cleaning, a robot vacuum shouldn't fully replace a traditional upright — think of it as handling daily light maintenance while you break out the upright periodically for a real deep clean. If your home is mostly hard flooring or low-pile rugs, a good robot vacuum can realistically handle the bulk of your cleaning needs.

Yes—but mainly in midrange and premium models with active obstacle recognition. Newer robots are noticeably better at avoiding visible cords, shoes, toys, and chair legs than older “bump-and-turn” models. Independent testing says obstacle avoidance has improved substantially, and current systems using cameras, structured light, or 3D sensors can often recognize and route around common floor clutter. rtings.com

Cords are less likely to be swallowed, but not impossible. A loose, thin, dark charging cable—especially lying partly under furniture or crossing a rug—remains difficult for many robots. Some current models explicitly advertise cord avoidance, but performance varies considerably by weak lighting. Even recent testing has found cheaper models dragging or catching cables. irobot.com

The answer is more mixed:

Flat, low-pile rugs: Usually much less troublesome than they used to be.  
Thick or shag rugs: Still a problem; the robot may fail to climb them, mistake the texture for an obstacle, or get the roller caught.  
Rug edges and tassels/fringe: Still among the worst-case scenarios. The issue is often mechanical—the brush physically grabs the fibers—rather than a failure to “see” the rug. Some newer robots can identify or avoid tasseled rugs, but you may lose cleaning coverage around the edge. support.dreametech.com

What matters more than “new”  
Look for:  
Camera + structured-light/3D obstacle avoidance, not just LiDAR mapping.  
Reviews specifically testing cords on carpet, not merely toys on bare floors.  
Tangle-resistant or redesigned brush rollers.  
App controls for no-go zones and rug/tassel avoidance.  
Adequate threshold and carpet-climbing clearance.  

A useful rule of thumb: a newer premium robot can often run unattended in a reasonably tidy home; a budget robot still benefits from having cords and fringe picked up first. No robot is reliably safe with loose earbuds, shoelaces, pet-toy strings, or long tassels.

Yes—but usually only modestly, and the word “HEPA” alone is not enough. A robot vacuum with genuine HEPA filtration can reduce the amount of fine dust, pollen, pet dander, and other particles it exhausts back into the room. EPA and ACAAI both recommend HEPA-filtered vacuums as one way to reduce airborne dust and allergen buildup. epa.gov

However, the benefit depends more on the entire dust-containment system than on the filter label. Sealed airflow is important because if air leaks around the filter, dust can bypass it. “HEPA filter” does not necessarily mean the whole robot is sealed. Dock design matters because emptying a bagless robot can release a concentrated puff of dust and allergens. A bagged, sealed self-emptying dock is generally preferable for allergy sufferers. Cleaning effectiveness varies since robots clean frequently, which can help prevent dust accumulation, but they may not deep-clean carpets as well as a powerful upright or canister vacuum. Air disturbance occurs because vacuuming can temporarily stir up allergens even when the exhaust is well filtered. EPA advises people with allergies or asthma to avoid being in the room while vacuuming. epa.gov Maintenance is also key because a clogged or poorly fitted filter, dirty brushes, and dusty bins reduce the practical benefit.

Research supports better particle control from HEPA-equipped machines, including robot vacuums, but evidence that HEPA vacuuming by itself produces large improvements in allergy or asthma symptoms is limited. One study found intensive HEPA vacuuming substantially reduced dust-mite allergen loading in carpets, while another found little reduction in personal allergen exposure during vacuuming. sciencedirect.com

Practical verdict: For someone with mild allergies, HEPA filtration is a worthwhile feature, especially if the robot runs daily while the home is empty. For significant allergies or asthma, prioritize this order: 1. Sealed system with independently reported low emissions 2. Bagged self-emptying dock 3. Effective carpet pickup and frequent operation 4. Genuinely high-efficiency/HEPA exhaust filter 5. Use a conventional sealed vacuum periodically for deep carpet cleaning, ideally while the allergy sufferer is away

So: meaningfully better than a poorly filtered or leaky robot, but not a substitute for good dust control or an air purifier—and “HEPA” by itself is mostly an incomplete marketing claim.

The bag itself is usually reliable; the auto-emptying pathway is a moderately common nuisance failure point, especially with pet hair, carpet fibers, fine dust, or debris that bridges the robot’s small dustbin outlet. It is more often a clog, poor seal, dirty filter, or sensor issue than a permanently failed motor.

Normal use means the dock empties the robot successfully for months or years, with the bag acting as a simple sealed consumable. The most common problem is that the bag is not full, but the robot only partially empties or does not empty at all because the chute, inlet, dock filter, or bag mouth is clogged. Roborock’s own troubleshooting specifically lists a full bag, missing or incorrectly installed bag, disabled emptying, and blocked pathways as causes. support.roborock.com Pet-hair homes face additional challenges. Short, dense hair can accumulate at the bag entrance instead of distributing through the bag, restricting airflow. Long-term testing has documented dock channels clogging with rolled-up hair and debris. vacuumwars.com False alerts or leakage can occur due to dirty sensors, a poorly seated bag, worn seals, or moisture entering the bag, leading to “bag full” warnings or dust leakage. iRobot notes that even its red bag indicator can mean either a full bag or a bag that is not properly detected. irobot.com Actual hardware failure of dock suction motors, switches, seals, and control electronics can eventually occur, but there is not good independent, model-wide data showing that bag docks commonly suffer catastrophic failure at a particular age.

I would rate the technology as reliable convenience feature: Yes. Completely maintenance-free: No. A reason to avoid self-emptying models: Usually no. A meaningful risk in a high-shedding pet household: Yes, particularly on designs with narrow or awkwardly shaped chutes.

The important distinction is that the dock adds another airflow system and several interfaces—robot outlet, dock ramp, bag collar, filter, fan, and sensors. A basic robot with a manually emptied bin has fewer things to obstruct or misread.

To improve the odds, choose a dock with a wide, accessible, cleanable air path. A removable dock base or visible chute is preferable; some newer models specifically advertise redesigned filters and removable bases to reduce clogging. us.roborock.com Avoid letting the robot’s onboard bin become tightly packed. In homes with pets, set the robot to empty more frequently or have it return mid-cycle. Use the correct bags and seat them firmly. Poorly fitting third-party bags can create leaks or airflow restrictions; manufacturers recommend genuine bags for proper fit and sealing. irobot.com Inspect the bag inlet and dock chute periodically, even if the app does not report a problem. Clean or replace filters as specified. A restricted filter can make the dock appear weak or cause incomplete emptying. irobot.com Buy from a manufacturer with good parts and warranty support. A dock failure is much more tolerable if replacement bags, filters, seals, or the dock itself are readily available.

Self-emptying bag docks are generally dependable, but clogging and imperfect emptying are common enough to consider them routine maintenance—not rare defects. For a mostly dust-and-crumb household, they are usually worth it. For multiple shedding pets, prioritize a robust, cleanable dock design and assume you may occasionally need to clear the chute manually.

Yes, the core technology of bagged self-emptying docks is mechanically reliable long-term, but it introduces frequent maintenance friction points. The high-powered suction motor inside the base station rarely suffers from catastrophic electrical or mechanical failure. However, self-emptying systems frequently suffer from clogs, sensor errors, and pressure leaks, which can make them feel unreliable if they aren't properly maintained.

The base station is mechanically simple, essentially a high-powered, stationary vacuum motor that runs for 15 to 30 seconds at a time. Unlike the robot, which relies on fragile drop sensors, LiDAR turrets, wheels, and drive motors, the base has fewer moving parts. Disposable paper or synthetic bags serve as both the container and the primary filter. Each time you replace the bag, you install a fresh filter, protecting the dock’s internal motor from fine dust buildup. By contrast, bagless self-emptying docks rely on washable filters that quickly clog, degrade suction, and fail more frequently over time.

While the base motor rarely dies, five issues often disrupt the system.

The first problem is airway clogs. The intake port on the bottom of the robot and the ramp leading into the dock have narrow 90-degree bends. High-volume debris like long pet hair, clumps of carpet fiber, leaf fragments, or pine needles can wedge in the throat of the dock. If a clog forms, the dock motor runs dry, fails to empty the robot's onboard bin, and can overheat if left unresolved.

The second issue is roller-to-dustbin jamming. If hair wraps tightly around the main brush roll or blocks the inner throat of the robot's internal dustbin, the dock's suction won't be strong enough to pull the hair out. The dock empties fine dust, but pet hair remains stuck inside the robot, causing the robot’s tiny bin to overflow during subsequent cleaning runs.

The third problem involves dirty infrared and optical sensors. Self-emptying docks use optical sensors to check if the dust bag is installed, if the bag is full, or if the robot is properly aligned. Over time, fine dust coats these sensors. This leads to constant false app alerts claiming the "Bag is Full," "Dock Airway is Blocked," or the robot refusing to empty at all.

The fourth issue is degradation of gaskets and seals. The auto-empty process relies on a tight vacuum seal between the dock's nozzle and the rubber gasket on the bottom or back of the robot vacuum. Over 2 to 4 years, these rubber gaskets dry out, crack, or collect grime. Air leaks past the seal, significantly reducing the suction power transferred from the dock to the robot bin.

The fifth problem is cheap third-party replacement bags. OEM bags can be expensive, leading users to buy cheap knockoff bags online. Low-quality third-party bags often tear under high suction or feature poor plastic collar seals. Fine dust escapes into the dock’s motor housing, eventually killing the base motor or dirtying internal components.

It is definitely worth it, provided you manage your expectations. A self-emptying bag system doesn't eliminate vacuum maintenance; it simply defers and consolidates it. Instead of manually dumping a tiny, dusty robot bin every single day, you only deal with the vacuum every 1 to 2 months.

To guarantee long-term reliability, stick to bagged docks. Avoid bagless auto-empty bases; bagged designs are far more reliable over a multi-year lifespan. If you have pets or long-haired family members, manually inspect the brush roll and the robot’s air inlet once every few weeks. Every time you swap the dust bag, wipe the dock’s rubber gaskets and optical sensors with a damp microfiber cloth. Buy quality replacement bags. Stick to OEM bags or high-rated, multi-layer synthetic third-party bags to protect the base motor.

Yes, HEPA filtration in a robot vacuum is meaningfully better for allergy sufferers—but only if the rest of the vacuum system supports it. Here is a breakdown of why HEPA filters make a difference, how robot vacuums affect indoor air quality, and the critical caveats you need to know before buying one.

Microscopic allergens—like dust mite feces, pet dander, pollen, and mold spores—range from 0.3 to 10 microns in size. Standard filters typically catch visible dust and hair, but they allow microscopic particles to pass straight through. When a vacuum runs, these tiny particles are blown out of the exhaust and into the air you breathe. True HEPA filters are certified to trap at least 99.97% of particles down to 0.3 microns. By capturing these microscopic irritants inside the filter rather than exhausting them back into your room, HEPA filtration prevents the vacuum from becoming a "dust blower."

Robot vacuums operate differently than traditional vacuums in ways that make HEPA filtration even more critical. Robot vacuums have exhaust vents located near the floor. As they move, bad exhaust filtration can blow settled dust up into the air column. HEPA exhaust ensures the blown air is clean. Allergy relief relies heavily on keeping baseline allergen levels low. Because robot vacuums can run automatically every day, they prevent dust and dander from building up in carpets and under furniture, which significantly reduces overall allergen loads in the home.

Having a HEPA filter in a robot vacuum does not automatically guarantee allergy relief. For it to be truly effective, you need to consider three main factors. A HEPA filter is useless if air can escape around the edges of the filter housing or through cracks in the vacuum body. Look for vacuums specified as having a Sealed HEPA System. Without a proper seal, unfiltered air bypasses the filter entirely. The small robot dustbins must be emptied frequently. Manually opening a tiny plastic bin over a trash can releases a cloud of concentrated dust and dander right into your face—negating the benefits of the HEPA filter. If you have moderate-to-severe allergies, pair a HEPA robot vacuum with a Self-Emptying Base Station that uses sealed, multi-layer filter bags (preferably HEPA-rated bags). These allow you to dispose of dust once every few weeks without ever exposing yourself to the airborne cloud. HEPA filters in robot vacuums are small and clog faster than those in full-sized vacuums. A clogged HEPA filter reduces suction power and can crack, allowing dust to leak through. Filters must be tapped out regularly and replaced every 2 to 6 months depending on pet ownership and usage.

If you are buying a robot vacuum specifically for allergy relief, look for a True HEPA Filter / Sealed HEPA System (captures 99.97% of 0.3-micron particles), an Auto-Empty Dock with Sealed Bags (avoids dust clouds when emptying), and high suction power / rubber brushes (rubber roller brushes tangle less with hair and agitate carpets better to pull up embedded dander). The Bottom Line: HEPA filtration in a robot vacuum is a meaningful upgrade for allergy sufferers, especially for daily maintenance. However, to get the full benefit, choose a model with a sealed air system and ideally an auto-empty station so you don't inhale dust when emptying it.

Not necessarily — for most homes, the sweet spot is actually $300–$600, not $1,000+. Here's the nuanced breakdown based on current testing data.  

At the premium tier, you're paying for genuinely different technology. At the $1,000+ tier, you're paying for the latest technology and the widest feature sets — this is where you'll find robotic arms that pick up objects off the floor, multi-pad mop switching systems that use fresh pads for each room, legs for climbing thresholds up to 80mm, and the most sophisticated AI-driven navigation. You also get hot-water mop washing, full all-in-one docks with wash, dry, auto-empty, and auto-refill, true AI obstacle avoidance with object recognition, and bigger batteries that handle 3,000+ sq ft on a single charge.  

But the mid-range has closed most of the gap. This is the key finding from current (2026) testing: the $300–$1,000 range is where robot vacuum value peaks in 2026 — this tier now includes models with LiDAR navigation, full-featured docks with self-emptying and mop washing, competitive mopping performance, and advanced obstacle avoidance, features that were exclusive to $1,500+ robots just two years ago. Price compression has made this the most competitive segment of the market.  

Even sub-$300 budget models have improved dramatically. One tested budget pick scored 90% in a carpet deep-clean test versus the 77% average across all tested robots — proof that a lower price tag doesn't automatically mean weaker cleaning. Another under-$300 model removed 100% of hair in a 7-inch hair-tangle test, compared to the average robot vacuum, which typically leaves about 38% tangled.  

A direct 2-week test comparing a $1,200 unit against a $550 unit found the pricier one had real edges — the $1,200 model offered excellent performance on hard floors and carpets, with a highly effective mopping mode and a simplifying dock, though despite being expensive it had occasional navigation issues. Meanwhile the $550 competitor offered strong cleaning and a good app, but its smart features were let down by poor navigation and high maintenance, frequently getting stuck and requiring constant supervision — showing that price alone doesn't guarantee a smooth experience.  

Testers consistently point to specific use cases rather than "everyone": If you have multi-level floors, pets, mixed carpeting and hard floors, or you just want minimal maintenance, this tier delivers luxury-box performance for mainstream homes. If pet hair is your biggest concern, it's recommended to get as expensive a robot vacuum as your budget allows. Budget vacuums generally have lower suction power and smaller dustbins than more expensive robot vacuums. One reviewer who tested extensively across price tiers concluded this is one category where you really do get what you pay for, though that doesn't mean you need to spend thousands on the latest flagship model — it's worth stretching your budget if you can.  

The key is knowing which features actually get cut and whether those trade-offs matter for your specific home — if you have a relatively simple floor plan without a lot of furniture obstacles, a budget robot can genuinely compete. It really depends on your home's layout — if you have hard floors and pets that shed a lot of hair, a robot vac could be a great addition, but if you have carpets and lots of obstacles that regularly need moving before every clean, it might not be worth the steep price tag (regardless of price paid). One reviewer directly argued against overspending: they struggled to see the utility in seriously flawed vacuum-mop combos with four-figure prices when simpler, more affordable units get the job done, noting a sub-$500 pick often discounted to half that price performs comparably to units three times as expensive.  

For a typical single-family home with normal clutter, 1-2 pets, and mixed flooring, a well-reviewed $300–$600 model will likely give you 85-90% of the premium experience — solid navigation, decent mopping, and self-emptying — without the four-figure price tag. The extra $400-700 for a $1,000+ model mainly pays off if you have a large multi-level house, heavy pet shedding, lots of floor clutter/obstacles, or you specifically want zero-maintenance automation (auto mop-washing, auto-refill, robotic arm pickup). If your home is straightforward, that premium money is often better spent elsewhere.

Self-emptying (auto-empty) systems are reliable enough to be mainstream, but they're also one of the more mechanically complex parts of a robot vacuum, and they do fail more often than the base robot itself — mostly for maintenance-related reasons rather than fundamental design flaws.

The core weak point is the dock's suction motor. A specialist repair site notes: the most common failure is the dock suction motor itself, which runs at high power and can burn out after 2–3 years of intensive use, especially when bags or canisters were not changed in time and the motor had to pull against extra resistance. That's a meaningful data point — roughly 2-3 years is when you should expect the auto-empty motor (not necessarily the robot itself) to be at risk.

Clogs are the second most common issue. A blocked air pathway — a tight plug of hair and dust — can shut the flow off completely, so the motor runs but dust stays in the robot. Over time, the valve at the robot bin outlet can jam shut, or the rubber seal at the dock junction can lose its elasticity, causing the system to lose vacuum at the connection.

Sensor/software false triggers also happen. Dirty or corroded contacts can mean the dock simply doesn't see the robot, and bag-full sensors can misfire, refusing to start a cycle even when the bag isn't actually full.

A general troubleshooting resource echoes this pattern, noting auto-empty dock failures usually trace to dirty docking contacts or the dust bag in the dock being full — i.e., mostly fixable maintenance issues, not catastrophic hardware death.

Real-world anecdotal evidence is mixed. Owner reports vary widely. One long-term user described a fairly severe failure: the self-emptying function worked great for about a year, but when new collection bags were needed, the self-emptying function stopped working — no matter how many times the bags were removed and replaced. Interestingly, it later intermittently worked again for short stretches, suggesting an intermittent connector, sensor, or seal fault rather than a single point of failure.

By contrast, other owners report the docking side (not emptying, but returning-to-dock) as the recurring nuisance rather than the bag mechanism itself: an occasional issue is that the vacuum struggles to get back onto its dock once cleaning is done, which is reportedly a fairly common issue with some brands, though it only happens a handful of times.

Even when working as designed, self-emptying systems have chronic annoyances that get conflated with "failure." Noise: many users report a jarring loud sound whenever the vacuum self-empties into the dock, with bursts that can reach up to 90 dB, louder than a blender.

Recurring consumable cost: most self-emptying systems rely on proprietary dust bags that must be replaced every month or two, adding ongoing costs that contradict the long-term convenience promise.

Internal buildup: despite being marketed as "self-emptying," these vacuums still require periodic cleaning, since hair and debris can clog the suction channel and the base interior needs regular cleaning to prevent odor or bacterial growth.

Auto-empty bag docks are best thought of as a genuinely useful convenience feature with a known, predictable wear-and-failure profile — not vaporware, but not "install and forget forever" either. The dock's internal blower motor is a legitimate wear item, with **~2-3 years** being a realistic ballpark before burnout risk rises under heavy use. **Clogs, seal degradation, and dirty contacts** cause the large majority of "it stopped emptying" complaints, and most are user-fixable with periodic cleaning rather than requiring a technician or replacement. Sensor/software glitches (false "bag full" readings, DND mode blocking cycles, dustbin cover not seated) account for many reported failures and are essentially non-issues once you know to check them. The **overall robot vacuum's usable lifespan is typically cited around 3–5 years** robot vacuums typically last between 3 to 5 years, depending on the brand, model, and how well they are maintained — so a dock motor failing in year 2-3 is a real risk factor within that window, but it's a repairable/replaceable subsystem, not something that necessarily kills the whole unit.

If you're deciding whether to trust the tech long-term: treat the auto-empty dock like any small appliance motor — expect to occasionally clean the air pathway and contacts, budget for eventual bag/motor issues after a couple of years of heavy use, and don't expect it to be truly "zero-maintenance" for its entire lifespan.
